name: Durrani Empire
info: The Afghan empire founded by Ahmad Shah Durrani in 1747, which conquered Punjab, Kashmir and Khorasan, crushed the Marathas at Panipat, and is counted the founding state of modern Afghanistan.

facts.capital: Kandahar; Kabul from Timur Shah's reign, with Peshawar as winter capital
facts.founder: Ahmad Shah Durrani, chosen by a loya jirga near Kandahar in 1747
facts.predecessor: The Afsharid Persia of Nader Shah, in whose army Ahmad commanded; the Hotak dynasty of the Ghilji; Mughal governors in Kabul and Peshawar
facts.successor: The Emirate of Afghanistan under Dost Muhammad Khan and the Barakzai dynasty; the Sikh Empire in Peshawar, Multan and Kashmir

t: In June 1747, after Nader Shah Afshar's death, a nine-day loya jirga near Kandahar chose Ahmad Khan of the Sadozai as Shah, and he renamed his Abdali tribe Durrani.
Ahmad Shah invaded India eight times, sacked Delhi in 1757 and on 14 January 1761 decisively defeated the Marathas at the Third Battle of Panipat, the high point of Afghan power.
His successors fought one another for the throne; by 1818 the Sadozai held little more than Kabul and its surroundings, and in 1823 the Barakzai displaced them.
dyk: When Ahmad Shah's envoy Khwaja Mirhan reached Beijing in 1763 he refused to kowtow to the Qianlong Emperor; the Qing read it as a claim of equality and cut ties with the Afghans, though the envoy himself was shown favour.
ev: After Nader Shah Afshar's death in June, a loya jirga near Kandahar lasting nine days chooses Ahmad Khan, crowned Padshah, Durr-i-Durran, by the holy man Sabir Khan.
The Mughal Emperor Ahmad Shah Bahadur cedes Sindh, the Punjab and the trans-Indus lands to Ahmad Shah to save his capital from attack.
Ahmad Shah sacks Delhi but leaves the Mughal emperor in nominal control in return for recognising Afghan suzerainty over Punjab, Sindh and Kashmir.
On 14 January the Durranis decisively defeat the Marathas under Sadashivrao Bhau at the Third Battle of Panipat, fought along a twelve-kilometre front.
Ahmad Shah crosses into Punjab for the sixth time, takes Amritsar, massacres thousands of Sikhs in the Vadda Ghallughara and destroys the Golden Temple.
Ahmad Shah dies in the mountains east of Kandahar; after Shah Wali Khan is assassinated at Farah, Timur Shah takes the throne in November.
On 7 June Shuja Shah signs the first Afghan pact with a European power, with the British East India Company; weeks later Mahmud Shah deposes him.
Ayub Shah, the last Sadozai ruler of the empire, is deposed and presumably killed.

sections.foundation:
Afghan independence had a forerunner: in 1709 Mirwais Hotak, chief of the Ghilji tribe, broke from the Safavids, and his son Mahmud Hotak ruled much of Iran from 1722 to 1725, until Nader Shah Afshar toppled the Hotaks in 1738. Ahmad Khan was the son of Muhammad Zaman Khan, chief of the Abdali tribe, and a commander of Nader Shah. When Nader Shah died in June 1747, Ahmad secured Kandahar and Ghazni, and a loya jirga, a grand council, met near Kandahar for nine days. Two chief contestants emerged, Hajji Jamal Khan of the Mohammadzai lineage and Ahmad Khan of the Sadozai. The holy man Mohammad Sabir Khan, who had predicted Ahmad's leadership, told the council that God had made him a greater man than any of them, placed sheaves of wheat or barley in his turban and crowned him Padshah, Durr-i-Durran, 'Pearl of the Pearls'. Ahmad renamed his tribe Durrani.

His first actions were to take Qalati Ghilji and Ghazni from the Ghilji and Kabul and Peshawar from the Mughal governor Nasir Khan. In 1749 the Mughal Emperor Ahmad Shah Bahadur ceded Sindh, the Punjab and the trans-Indus lands to save his capital. Ahmad then turned west to Mashhad, whose ruler Shahrukh Afshar acknowledged Afghan suzerainty, and sent an army north of the Hindu Kush that brought the Tajik, Hazara, Uzbek, Turkmen and other peoples of northern Afghanistan under his control. The year 1747 marks the appearance of an Afghan state independent of both the Persian and Mughal empires.
sections.socioeconomy:
The empire was a tribal state held together by its founder's management of Pashtun alliances and by the plunder of India. Ahmad Shah's eight invasions brought Kashmir and most of the Punjab under Afghan rule, with Lahore governed by Afghans, and the sack of Delhi in 1757 yielded the booty he coveted; the Mughal emperor was left in nominal control of his city as long as he acknowledged Afghan suzerainty south of the Indus up to the Sutlej. Ahmad was credited with balancing tribal alliances and hostilities to a remarkable degree and with directing tribal energies away from rebellion. That balance was later upset by his grandson Zaman Shah, who replaced Barakzai leaders with men of his own Sadozai lineage.

The empire's reach was fixed by negotiation as much as conquest. Rebellions in the north around Bukhara led Ahmad Shah and the Uzbek Emir of Bukhara to agree that the Amu Darya would divide their lands, and he may have sought a similar sphere of influence with the Qing, as he had with the Ottomans, who divided Iran with him. In 1763 he occupied the lands between Tashkent and Kokand at the plea of Fazil Biy of Kokand and Kyrgyz chieftains against Qing expansion, withdrawing by 1764 when no alliance formed, and sent an embassy to Beijing with a letter, probably a fath-nama celebrating Panipat, and gifts of four horses, painted by the Qing court painter Giuseppe Castiglione.
sections.military:
The Durrani army was built on cavalry armed with flintlocks, which made hit-and-run attacks combining new firearms with Turco-Mongol tactics. Its core was 10,000 mounted ghulams, slave-soldiers carrying the sher-bacha blunderbuss, a third of them former Shia Qizilbash soldiers of Nader Shah. The bulk of the army was irregular tribal cavalry armed with lance and broadsword; infantry and artillery played very small roles, apart from the zamburak, light swivel guns mounted on camels. Ahmad Shah was famous for winning wars against much larger armies. When the Marathas under Raghunathrao drove Timur Shah from Lahore, Multan and Kashmir in 1757, Ahmad declared a jihad, gathering warriors of many Afghan tribes and the Baloch under Mir Nasir Khan I, Khan of Kalat.

By 1759 his army had reached Lahore, and on 14 January 1761 it decisively defeated the Marathas under Sadashivrao Bhau at the Third Battle of Panipat, fought along a twelve-kilometre front between largely Muslim and largely Hindu armies. The Sikhs proved harder to subdue. In 1762 Ahmad crossed the passes for the sixth time, took Amritsar, massacred thousands of Sikhs in the Vadda Ghallughara and destroyed the Golden Temple; within two years the Sikhs rebelled again and rebuilt their holy city, and his later attempts to subjugate them failed. In 1768 Shah Wali Khan invaded Badakhshan and seized Fayzabad, and within the year Ahmad occupied the country and executed its ruler Sultan Shah.
sections.governance:
The Shah ruled through the tribal order that had chosen him. Kandahar was the capital; under Timur Shah the court moved to Kabul, with Peshawar as its winter seat. Succession was contested at every death. Ahmad named his son Timur Shah heir over the elder Sulaiman Shah, whom he thought violent and unpopular with the Kandahari Durranis; after his death in 1772 Shah Wali Khan and Sardar Jahan Khan concealed it, carried the body to Kandahar and proclaimed Sulaiman. Timur marched from Herat, Shah Wali and his sons were assassinated at Farah, Sulaiman surrendered, and Timur took the throne in November 1772.

When Timur died in 1793 three of his sons, governors of Kandahar, Herat and Kabul, contended for the throne; Zaman Shah, holding the capital, won at twenty-three and imprisoned many half-brothers. The Sadozai efforts to impose an absolute monarchy on the Pashtun tribes without the advice of the other tribal leaders failed. Zaman owed his throne to the Barakzai chief Painda Khan but executed him and the chiefs of the Nurzai, Alizai and Qizilbash; Painda Khan's son backed Zaman's brother Mahmud Shah, who took Kandahar without bloodshed, defeated Zaman in 1801 and had his eyes lanced. Mahmud ruled from 1801 to 1803 and 1809 to 1818, Shuja Shah from 1803 to 1809, Abbas Mirza briefly in 1810, Sultan Ali Shah in 1818–1819 and Ayub Shah from 1819 to 1823.
sections.impact:
The Durrani Empire is considered the foundational polity of the modern nation-state of Afghanistan, and Ahmad Shah, remembered as Ahmad Shah Baba, its Father of the Nation. At its peak it ruled present-day Afghanistan, much of Pakistan, parts of Iran, eastern Turkmenistan and north-western India. Its victory at Panipat in 1761 broke the Maratha advance into north-western India, while the Mughal emperors became nominal heads of Delhi under Afghan suzerainty.

The empire also redrew its neighbours' ambitions. The Amu Darya became the agreed border with Bukhara, and the Qing, after Ahmad's embassy of 1763 and his conquest of Badakhshan in 1768, abandoned the pretence that the Afghans were tributaries: the Qianlong Emperor refused Sultan Shah of Badakhshan any aid and in effect recognised the Afghans as a rival power, gambling on the difficult terrain between the two realms for safety. The Durrani wars against the Sikhs, including the massacre of the Vadda Ghallughara in 1762, were followed by the rebuilding of Amritsar and, under Ranjit Singh, by the rise of the Sikh Empire that took Peshawar, Multan and Kashmir from the Afghans. The treaty Shuja Shah signed with the British East India Company on 7 June 1809, the first Afghan pact with a European power, pledged joint action against Franco-Persian aggression and foreshadowed the British restoration of Shuja in 1839 and the First Anglo-Afghan War.
sections.decline:
The empire began to unravel before its founder died. From 1762 his hold loosened: parts of the Punjab were lost to the Sikhs, and northern territories to the Uzbeks, forcing the compromise on the Amu Darya. Ahmad Shah died in the mountains east of Kandahar in 1772. His successors governed so ineptly amid profound unrest that within fifty years the empire as such was at an end and Afghanistan was in civil war. The quarrels among Timur Shah's sons after 1793 gave outside powers their pretext to intervene; Zaman Shah's purge of Barakzai chiefs brought his overthrow and blinding in 1801, and Ranjit Singh, who had wrested power from Zaman's forces in Punjab, gave him asylum.

Zaman's fall opened a period of even greater violence: Mahmud Shah's first reign lasted two years before Shuja Shah replaced him; Shuja's treaty with the East India Company in June 1809 was followed within weeks by his deposition; Mahmud's second reign ended when his brother deposed him in 1818; Sultan Ali Shah was strangled by his brother Isma'il, and the Durranis lost Kashmir to the Sikh Empire at the Battle of Shopian in 1819. By 1818 the Sadozai controlled little more than Kabul and the territory within 160 kilometres of it, having alienated the other Durrani lineages. Ayub Shah was deposed and presumably killed in 1823, and Dost Muhammad Khan and the Barakzai dynasty deposed the Sadozai in Kabul, superseding the empire with the Emirate of Afghanistan. A Sadozai line held Herat until 1863.

summary: The Durrani Empire (1747–1823) was built by Ahmad Shah Durrani from the wreck of Nader Shah's Persia into a Pashtun state reaching from Khorasan to the Punjab, victorious over the Marathas at Panipat in 1761 but unable to hold down the Sikhs. Succession wars among his descendants left the Sadozai with little beyond Kabul before the Barakzai displaced them.
references: Mountstuart Elphinstone, An Account of the Kingdom of Caubul, and Its Dependencies in Persia, Tartary and India (Longman, Hurst, Rees, Orme, and Brown, 1815)
Jonathan L. Lee, Afghanistan: A History from 1260 to the Present (Reaktion Books, 2022)
Ganda Singh, Ahmad Shah Durrani: Father of Modern Afghanistan (Asia Publishing House, 1959)

Juul Eijk and Timur Khan, ''Do You Not Bow before Heaven?': The First Qing-Durrani Encounter, the Tributary Non-relationship, and Disorder on a Shared Frontier', Journal of the Economic and Social History of the Orient 66 (2023)

notes: The article's lead says the Marathas controlled eastern Afghanistan in 1749 after driving out the Mughals, while its body says the Mughal emperor ceded Sindh and Punjab to Ahmad that year and the Marathas ousted Timur Shah from Lahore in 1757; the body's account is followed.
The article does not say who deposed Mahmud Shah in 1818 beyond 'his brother'; left unnamed.
The article does not date Dost Muhammad Khan's accession; the 1823 point ties the Barakzai supersession to Ayub Shah's deposition, as the register's end year does.
Timur Shah's reign (1772–1793) has no narrative in the article beyond the move of the capital to Kabul, so the socioeconomy and governance sections say little of it.
